title: Toolboxes and the managed MCP endpoint
summary: A toolbox curates tools once and exposes them behind one managed MCP-compatible endpoint with central authentication, guardrails and versioning. Any MCP client can use it, not only Foundry agents.
useIf: Several agents or runtimes share tools, and you want one credential, governance and release point.
avoidIf: The tool is not toolbox-eligible or must execute inside your own process.

explain.md: A **toolbox** is a managed resource that groups tools behind a single MCP-compatible endpoint. It centralizes authentication (Entra ID and OAuth identity passthrough), applies guardrails at toolbox level and supports **versioning**: create a version, test it, promote it to default, and every consuming agent picks it up with no redeploy [[r3]]. Toolboxes are created in Foundry but are not limited to Foundry agents: any MCP-compatible runtime can consume one, including Agent Framework, LangGraph or custom code [[r3]]. In Agent Framework hosted agents use `FoundryToolbox` in Python or `AddFoundryToolboxes` in .NET [[r2]].

explain.title: One endpoint in front of many tools
explain.alt: Prompt agents, hosted agents, Agent Framework and other MCP clients connect to one toolbox endpoint, which fronts MCP servers, OpenAPI tools, search, code interpreter and A2A agents.

What you do
Status

explain.md: **Tool search** matters because every tool definition sent with a request adds input tokens, competes for context and can lower selection accuracy when hundreds of tools are present [[r3]]. Tool search and skills work only through a toolbox [[r3]]. Auth options for tools and remote MCP servers are key-based, Entra (agent identity or project managed identity), OAuth identity passthrough (OBO) and unauthenticated where appropriate [[r1]].

explain.title: Not everything fits in a toolbox
explain.md: In a toolbox: MCP, web search, Azure AI Search, code interpreter, file search, OpenAPI, A2A, browser automation, Fabric IQ and Work IQ. Direct integration only: function calling (client-side execution), Grounding with Bing, computer use, image generation, SharePoint, Fabric data agent and Azure Functions [[r3]].

whereToUse: A platform team publishing an approved tool catalog for many agent teams
Mixed runtimes (prompt agents, hosted agents, Agent Framework, LangGraph) that must share the same tools
Releasing a tool change once and rolling it out to every consumer through version promotion
Catalogs large enough that sending every tool definition would waste context (tool search, preview)

use: More than one agent needs the same tools
You want credentials and guardrails in one governed place
You want to promote tool versions without redeploying agents
avoid: A single agent with one private tool and no reuse: direct integration is less to manage
The tool is on the direct-only list (for example SharePoint or computer use)
Execution must stay in your process: use function calling
flips: Catalog grows to dozens or hundreds of tools: add tool search, accepting preview status
A tool needs per-user identity: use OAuth identity passthrough (OBO) so the user's permissions apply
Policy forbids preview features: use toolbox without tool search or skills

pitfalls.symptom: Model picks the wrong tool or ignores the right one
pitfalls.cause: Hundreds of tool definitions compete for context and selection accuracy drops
pitfalls.fix: Use tool search (preview) with pinned critical tools and organization terms as added context [[r3]].

pitfalls.symptom: A tool call returns 401 although the toolbox is configured
pitfalls.cause: The token audience is the MCP server URL rather than the downstream resource ID
pitfalls.fix: Set the audience to the resource ID such as `https://storage.azure.com` [[r4]].

pitfalls.symptom: Consumers broke after a tool update
pitfalls.cause: A new toolbox version was promoted to default without testing
pitfalls.fix: Create a version, test it, then promote. Skills are immutable per version, so pin the one you tested [[r3]].

scenarios.title: Platform team serving many agents
scenarios.situation: A platform team supports ten agent teams that use five common tools. Credentials must be managed centrally and tool changes must roll out without redeploying agents.
unknowns: Do any tools need per-user identity?
Is preview allowed for tool search?
scenarios.question: How do you expose the tools?

options.name: One toolbox with versioned promotion
options.why: One endpoint, central auth and guardrails, and promoting a default version updates every consumer.
options.tradeoff: A new governed resource that must be tested before each promotion.

options.name: Copy each tool configuration into every agent
options.why: Credentials and configs drift across ten teams and a change needs ten redeploys.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a single agent with one private tool.

options.name: Plain MCP server connection per agent
options.why: Reuses the server and is simple to start.
options.tradeoff: No grouping, versioning or toolbox-level guardrails.

flips.if: The catalog grows to hundreds of tools
flips.then: Add tool search (preview) so tool definitions do not flood context.

flips.if: Only one agent uses the tools
flips.then: Direct integration is less to manage.

scenarios.takeaway: Toolboxes pay off when sharing and release control matter.

scenarios.title: Tool that is not toolbox-eligible
scenarios.situation: An agent must search a SharePoint site and drive a browser UI through computer use. The platform team wants everything in the toolbox.
constraints: SharePoint and computer use are required
unknowns: Is there an alternative route to the SharePoint content, such as a knowledge base?
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Use direct tool integration for those tools and keep the rest in the toolbox
options.why: SharePoint and computer use appear in the direct-only column of the support table.
options.tradeoff: Two paths to govern, and those tools sit outside toolbox versioning.

options.name: Insist on the toolbox for all tools
options.why: The toolbox does not support those tools, so the requirement cannot be met.
options.tradeoff: Right for tools in the supported list.

options.name: Wrap them as client-side functions
options.why: You can reach the same systems from your own code.
options.tradeoff: You build, secure and run the wrappers, and the optimizer cannot evaluate their execution.

flips.if: SharePoint content can come through a Foundry IQ knowledge base
flips.then: Consume the knowledge base instead of the direct tool.

flips.if: The tool list in the docs expands to include them

scenarios.takeaway: Check the support table before you standardize on a path.

quiz.q: Match each tool to where the docs say it can be used.
quiz.explain: Code interpreter is in both columns. SharePoint, computer use and Azure Functions are direct only. Function calling executes client-side. Tool search and skills exist only through a toolbox.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to add tool search to a large toolbox?
options: It removes the need for authentication
It keeps tool definitions out of the context until needed
It lets function calling run server-side
quiz.explain: Tool search hides tools by default and exposes `tool_search` and `call_tool`, which saves input tokens and improves selection. It does not change execution speed, auth or function calling. It is preview.
Toolboxes front tools with one endpoint, support version promotion and centralize auth and guardrails. Any MCP-compatible client can consume them, so they are not Foundry-only.

flashcards.front: What does a Foundry toolbox give you that a plain MCP server does not?
flashcards.back: Curated grouping, central auth, toolbox-level guardrails, versioning with promotion to default, and (preview) tool search and skills.

flashcards.front: Which tools cannot be added to a toolbox?
flashcards.back: Function calling (client-side), Grounding with Bing, computer use, image generation, SharePoint, Fabric data agent and Azure Functions. Use direct integration.
